name: Inverse normal distribution
seoDesc: Inverse normal distribution: work out your result from the probability and the mean. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary:
Give the Inverse normal distribution calculator the probability, the mean and the standard deviation and it returns the answer. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number.

The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Inverse normal distribution calculator work?
sections.html:
The Inverse normal distribution calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select the desired type of tail area); then you type in the probability (p), the mean (μ) and the standard deviation (σ).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.html:
• A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as P(X < x) = p, P(X > x) = p and P(|X − μ| > x) = p. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

sections.title: The formula behind the Inverse normal distribution calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

X=(probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))
X=(1 − probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))
X=the smaller of (the absolute value of (mean (μ) − ((1 ÷ 2) × probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))), the absolute value of (mean (μ) − (1 − 1 ÷ 2 × probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))))
X₁ (Left tail upper bound)=mean (μ) − the smaller of (the absolute value of (mean (μ) − ((1 ÷ 2) × probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))), the absolute value of (mean (μ) − (1 − 1 ÷ 2 × probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))))
X₂ (Right tail lower bound)=mean (μ) + the smaller of (the absolute value of (mean (μ) − ((1 ÷ 2) × probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))), the absolute value of (mean (μ) − (1 − 1 ÷ 2 × probability (p), mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))))
X=-mean (μ) + ((1 ÷ 2) × probability (p) + 1 ÷ 2, mean (μ), standard deviation (σ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Inverse normal distribution calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the probability, the mean and the standard deviation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Inverse normal distribution calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the probability, the mean and the standard deviation, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Inverse normal distribution calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
